text: A hardcoded secret is any credential -- a database password, an API key, a storage connection string -- typed directly into source code or a plain-text config file instead of retrieved from a dedicated secret store at runtime. It's an easy mistake: you paste the real value in to get something working, and mean to replace it later. Later often doesn't come before that file gets committed.

Once that line exists in a file tracked by Git, the secret isn't just in the code -- it's in every place that code travels. And deleting it in a later commit doesn't remove it. Git history keeps every past commit, so the plain-text value is still sitting there for anyone who runs git log against old commits.

It leaks beyond the repo too. A CI/CD pipeline step that echoes a variable for debugging can print the secret straight into build logs. If the code ships in a container image, the secret is baked into one of that image's layers, shipped with every pull from the registry. And public repos are scanned continuously by automated tools hunting for credential-shaped strings.

The real fix isn't being more careful about typing -- it's never writing the secret into the file at all. Retrieve it at runtime from a dedicated secret store instead, so there's nothing sensitive for Git history, CI logs, or a container image to ever capture in the first place. The application code changes very little: instead of a literal password, it calls a function that asks a secret store for the current value by name, every time it runs.

That's the standard the rest of this chapter builds toward. Next: Azure Key Vault, where a secret like a connection string or API key is stored properly, an app retrieves it at runtime through a managed identity instead of a hardcoded credential, and an access policy controls exactly who -- and what service -- is allowed to read it at all.
